passage: Diego's family in Valencia says one short thank-you before dinner, all holding hands. Diego, ten, usually rushes it so he can eat. Tonight his friend Emeka was staying over. Emeka's family says theirs silently, eyes closed. When Diego's father said, "Shall we?", Emeka looked unsure. Diego's mother smiled. "You can say yours your way, love." So Emeka bowed his head quietly while the others spoke. Diego peeked at him. Emeka looked so calm that Diego slowed down for once and actually thought about the words. After the meal, he asked Emeka what he thought about during the quiet. "Mostly my mum's cooking," Emeka said. "And today, your mum."

qa.q: How does Diego's family say thank-you before dinner?
qa.a: They say one short thank-you together while holding hands.

qa.q: Why did Diego slow down during the thank-you tonight?
qa.a: Watching how calm Emeka looked in his quiet prayer made Diego curious and made him want to mean the words instead of rushing them.

qa.q: How did Diego's mother help Emeka feel included?
qa.a: She invited him to give thanks in his own way, so he could join the moment without having to copy a practice that was not his family's.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel about the evening?
qa.a: He likely felt welcome and grateful, since his quiet habit was respected and he even included Diego's mum in his thanks. 🙂

grounding: It shows children taking part in a short family gratitude ritual and noticing what reflection feels like.

passage: The hostel warden at the boys' school rang a small bell at six each evening. For two minutes, everyone in the study hall sat still. Noor, eleven and new, hated it at first. His leg jiggled. He peeked at the clock. Zubin, the older boy beside him, kept his eyes closed and his hands loose on the desk. On the fourth evening, Noor tried it too. He heard the fan, a crow outside, someone's stomach growling. He nearly laughed. Then he thought of his mother's voice on the phone the night before, and his chest felt warm and tight at once. When the bell rang again, Zubin nudged him. "Better?" Noor shrugged, but he didn't reach for his pen straight away.

qa.q: How long did the evening silence in the study hall last?
qa.a: It lasted two minutes, starting and ending with a small bell.

qa.q: What does Noor's warm and tight chest suggest when he thinks of his mother?
qa.a: It suggests he misses home and is grateful for her at the same time; the quiet gave space for feelings he had been pushing aside.

qa.q: How could the warden help new boys like Noor settle into the silence?
qa.a: He could tell them it is fine to fidget at first and suggest one simple thing to notice, like sounds or someone they are thankful for.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Noor's shrug at the end?
qa.a: He might read it as a quiet yes, since Noor didn't grab his pen right away, and feel glad the new boy is settling in.

grounding: It shows a boy slowly joining a short daily silence practice at a hostel and finding a moment of reflection.

passage: I'm Kamal, and my little brother Yogesh is eight. Our Nani lights the lamp every morning and says a short prayer. Yogesh used to run past, looking for his socks. This month something changed. I saw him stop at the doorway, fold his hands and stand still while Nani sang. He doesn't know all the words, so he moves his lips a bit late. Yesterday he put a marigold near the lamp, one he had picked from the neighbour's pot, which Nani pretended not to notice. At night he whispers to himself before sleeping. I asked him once what he says. He said, "Just thank you. For today." I can't tell if he means it the way Nani does, but he seems calmer.

qa.q: What did Yogesh put near the lamp yesterday?
qa.a: He put a marigold he had picked from the neighbour's pot.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's whispering at night suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he has started his own small gratitude habit, thanking the day in his own words, which may make him feel calm.

qa.q: How could Nani gently support Yogesh's new habit?
qa.a: She could teach him one or two lines of the prayer slowly, or invite him to light the lamp with her, without making him feel tested.

qa.q: Why might Kamal be unsure about what the prayer means to Yogesh?
qa.a: Kamal only sees the outside, the folded hands and whispers, so he can guess Yogesh is calmer but cannot know what he feels inside.

grounding: An older sibling observes a younger child beginning to join a family prayer and a simple gratitude habit.

passage: Sunday: At bedtime, after Rashmi lit the small lamp by the photo of Ajji, she said, 'Let's say three good things from today, Jeevan.' He was eight and grumpy after losing at carrom. 'Nothing was good.' She just said hers and switched off the light. Thursday: The lamp flickered again. Jeevan sat with his knees pulled up, eyes closed for a moment the way Amma did. 'Okay. One: Ma'am let me feed the class fish. That's all.' Rashmi smiled in the dark. Next Tuesday: Rashmi was tired and forgot. Jeevan tugged her sleeve. 'Amma, lamp first. Then my three. I've got four today, actually.' He counted them on his fingers, slowly, before falling asleep.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say was his one good thing on Thursday?
qa.a: His teacher let him feed the class fish.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan say 'Nothing was good' on Sunday?
qa.a: He was grumpy after losing at carrom, so he didn't feel like finding anything good in his day.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's way of starting the habit work?
qa.a: She didn't force him; she simply kept doing it herself each night so he could join when ready.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt when Jeevan reminded her on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was probably touched and pleased that the small ritual had become his own. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child gradually taking part in a nightly lamp ritual and gratitude practice.

passage: Vaibhav, you think sitting quietly is punishment, no? I thought the same when I was ten. Every morning my grandfather sat by the river near our town before his puja, and one day he made me come. 'Just sit. Say nothing. Listen,' he said. I fidgeted so much! I counted ants. I sighed loudly. He didn't scold, just kept sitting. After some days I began to hear things: the washerman's slap-slap on stones, a kingfisher diving, my own breath. Then he said, 'Now think of one thing you're thankful for.' I said, 'Mangoes.' He laughed so much. But every morning after that I had one thing. Try with me tomorrow, before school. Only five minutes.

qa.q: What sounds did the narrator begin to hear by the river?
qa.a: The washerman's slapping on stones, a kingfisher diving and the narrator's own breath.

qa.q: How was the narrator feeling during the first days of sitting by the river?
qa.a: Restless and bored; the narrator fidgeted, counted ants and sighed loudly.

qa.q: What worked in the grandfather's way of teaching silence?
qa.a: He kept sitting calmly without scolding and then added a simple gratitude question once the child had settled.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav find it easier to try with the narrator than alone?
qa.a: Hearing that the narrator was also restless at that age makes it feel less like punishment and more like something shared.

grounding: An elder recalls learning a short silence and gratitude practice as a child alongside a family ritual.

passage:
Every evening at seven, Mohit's family in Nagpur lit a lamp and sat in silence for one minute, then each said one thing they were thankful for.
Tonight the power had gone, and a wedding band was blaring down the street. His friend Elizabeth was visiting.
“Can we skip it tonight?” Mohit's little brother asked.
Mohit, ten, shook his head. He lit the lamp with a matchstick. He closed his eyes. The trumpets were so loud he nearly laughed.
After the minute, he said, “I'm thankful for Elizabeth coming.”
Elizabeth hesitated, then folded her hands. “In my house we say grace. Can I say mine?”
Mohit's mother smiled. “Please.”

qa.q: What did Mohit's family do every evening at seven?
qa.a: They lit a lamp and sat in silence for one minute, then each said one thing they were thankful for.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel keeping the minute of silence during the noise?
qa.a: He felt calm but amused, nearly laughing at the loud trumpets.

qa.q: Why was it good for the family to keep the habit even on a noisy night?
qa.a: It showed the habit mattered, and made space for Elizabeth to share her own prayer.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when invited to say her grace?
qa.a: She probably feels welcomed and respected for her own tradition.

grounding: A ten-year-old keeps his family's gratitude minute during a noisy power cut and welcomes a friend's prayer.

passage:
On the shelf in Pranav's bedroom in Bengaluru was a glass jar full of folded paper slips.
Every night, before sleep, his mother Madhuri sat on the edge of his bed. “Three things?”
Pranav, nine, thought. “Hot idli at breakfast. Kunal lent me his blue pencil. And the rain stopped before football.”
He wrote them on a slip and dropped it in the jar.
Some nights he couldn't think of anything and felt grumpy. Then Madhuri would say, “Just one small thing.” And he always found one.
On his birthday, they opened the jar and read the slips together. Pranav laughed at how many were about food.

qa.q: What did Pranav drop into the jar?
qa.a: He dropped a slip with three things he was thankful for.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel on nights when he couldn't think of anything?
qa.a: He felt grumpy until his mother suggested just one small thing.

qa.q: Why does the gratitude jar help Pranav?
qa.a: It helps him notice small good things each day and remember them later.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel reading the slips on his birthday?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and amused, seeing his happy memories.

grounding: A nine-year-old keeps a nightly gratitude habit with his mother.

passage:
“Payal, why are you sitting with your eyes closed? The bus comes in ten minutes.”
“Two minutes of quiet, Eshaan. Then I'll go.”
“Are you praying?”
“Sometimes. Sometimes I just breathe and think about the day.”
“Boring.”
“It's not. It helps me not be grumpy.”
Eshaan sat down next to her. “Show me.”
“Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Out. Think of one thing you're glad about.”
Eshaan was quiet. Then he said, “The bus is late. I'm glad.”
Payal laughed. “Close enough.”

qa.q: How long does Payal sit quietly?
qa.a: Two minutes.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about her morning quiet time?
qa.a: She feels calmer and less grumpy because of it.

qa.q: What makes Payal's quiet time an easy habit for Eshaan to try?
qa.a: It is short, simple and flexible, whether praying or just breathing and thinking.

qa.q: How does Eshaan's view of the habit change?
qa.a: He starts by calling it boring, then becomes curious and tries it.

grounding: An eleven-year-old keeps a short silence and gratitude habit and shares it with her brother.

passage:
When I was ten, I used to eat lunch with Francis. Before he ate, he always closed his eyes for a moment. I thought it was weird.
One day I asked. He said, "I say thanks. For the food, and for Mummy who made it."
The next day I tried it, secretly. I just thought, "Thanks, Amma, for the lemon rice." It felt silly. Then it felt nice.
Now I'm older, and I still do it. Just a pause, a few seconds of quiet, before I eat.
My name is Kiran, and I learnt that small habit from a boy in Class 5.

qa.q: What did Kiran silently thank Amma for?
qa.a: The lemon rice.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling the first time trying the pause?
qa.a: Kiran felt silly at first, then found it pleasant and calming.

qa.q: How could Kiran pass on this habit?
qa.a: Kiran could share it with a friend or younger cousin the way Francis did, just by explaining it simply.

qa.q: How might Francis feel if he knew Kiran still does it?
qa.a: Francis would probably feel touched and pleased that a small habit of his mattered.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Girls' Block.
Every morning we have five minutes of silence before breakfast. Most girls fidget. Leela, who joined this term, used to giggle and whisper through it.
This week I noticed a change. She sits cross-legged, eyes closed, hands in her lap. After, she writes in a small notebook.
Today I asked what she writes. She said, "Three good things from yesterday. My Nani told me to." Today's list: "Hot water in the bathroom. Sumit Sir's funny joke in maths. A letter from home."
I've asked if she'd share the idea at Sunday assembly. She agreed, a little shyly. — Mrs Varghese

passage:
Dear Diary,
Tonight Kalyani paati lit the lamp and sat quietly, like she does every evening. Usually I watch TV. Today the power was off, so I sat with her.
She didn't talk. She just breathed and looked at the flame. I sat too. It was boring for two minutes. Then my brain slowed down.
After, she asked, "What are you thankful for today?"
I said, "The power cut." She laughed!
Then I said properly: "You. And that my test went okay. And the mango pickle."
She held my hand. I think I'll sit with her again tomorrow, even if the power is on.
— Mehak

qa.q: What did Kalyani paati light every evening?
qa.a: The lamp.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling after the first two minutes of silence?
qa.a: Mehak felt calmer and more settled as the boredom passed.

qa.q: What small habit could Mehak keep from this evening?
qa.a: Sitting quietly with paati for a few minutes and naming a few things to be thankful for.

qa.q: How might Kalyani paati feel when Mehak says "You"?
qa.a: Kalyani paati is likely touched and warm ❤️, hearing that her grandchild is thankful for her.

grounding: During a power cut, a child joins her grandmother's evening silence and gratitude.

Every morning before school, Kalyani goes with her grandmother to light the lamp at the tulsi in their courtyard. They stand quietly for a minute, then Kalyani says three things she's thankful for, out loud but softly. Today it was: the rain last night, Paati's knee not hurting, and the new pencil box.
Noor, from the next house, came to walk with her to school and waited by the gate. Kalyani's Paati waved her in. "Stand with us if you like, child."
Noor stood, a little shy. When they finished, Noor said, "At home, Nana says thanks before eating too. In his own words."
Kalyani grinned. "Tomorrow you tell one thing." Noor thought about it all the way to the bus stop.

passage:
On Chuseok morning, Soo-ah's family set up the table for the ancestral rite in their Seoul apartment: rice cakes, pears, fish, a photo of Grandma in the middle. Her cousin Sami, visiting from Busan, kept poking the pears and whispering jokes.
When they bowed, Soo-ah kept her forehead on the floor longer than usual. She thought about Grandma teaching her to fold dumplings last Chuseok and her floury hands. She felt her throat get tight.
Afterwards Sami asked, "Why were you down there so long?"
"I was saying thank you," Soo-ah said. "For the dumplings."
Sami was quiet. At the next bow, he stayed still too, with his eyes shut, and didn't poke anything.

qa.q: Whose photo was in the middle of the table?
qa.a: A photo of Grandma was in the middle of the table.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling while she bowed?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt grateful and a little sad, missing Grandma, which is why her throat got tight.

qa.q: How could an adult help a fidgety child like Sami take part in the rite?
qa.a: An adult could quietly explain what the bow means and suggest one person to think of, so it feels real rather than boring.

qa.q: How does Sami's view of the rite change after Soo-ah explains?
qa.a: Sami seems to see it as a real moment of remembering, not a ritual to joke through, so he joins in quietly.

grounding: Illustrates a child using a family ritual as a moment of silent gratitude and remembrance.

passage:
In January, the school started one minute of silence after lunch. Everyone put heads down; then you could write one line in a gratitude notebook. Sachin thought it was pointless. He doodled cricket bats instead.
Manoj, at the next desk, wrote something every day and never showed anyone.
Then came a bad Thursday. Sachin failed a maths test and got shouted at in PE. At the silence, he put his head down just to hide his face. The room was quiet. The heater ticked. After a while his shoulders stopped feeling like rocks.
When the bell went, he opened the notebook and wrote, slowly: "Manoj lent me his jumper at PE."
Manoj saw, and grinned, and didn't say anything.

qa.q: What did Sachin write in the notebook on Thursday?
qa.a: He wrote, "Manoj lent me his jumper at PE."

qa.q: Why did Sachin put his head down on the bad Thursday?
qa.a: Sachin felt upset and embarrassed after failing a maths test and being shouted at, so he wanted to hide his face.

qa.q: What small change could help students who find the silence pointless?
qa.a: The school could explain it isn't a test; you can just rest, and nobody checks what you write.

qa.q: If you were Manoj, what would you want after seeing Sachin's line?
qa.a: You'd probably feel pleased and touched, and want to keep it quiet so Sachin doesn't feel embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child slowly finding value in a short school practice of silence and gratitude.

passage:
I'm Sunaina, Manoj's elder sister. Since the harvest festival this January, something changed in my brother.
Every night before dinner, Manoj, nine, closes his eyes for a moment. He doesn't say a prayer out loud. He just sits still, hands folded on the table, while the rest of us reach for rotis. Once I heard him whisper, "Thank you for the rain and for Amma's dal."
Our cousin Prem laughed. "Are you a monk now?"
Manoj opened his eyes, smiled, and said, "It's quiet time." He didn't get upset.
I don't know what he thinks about in that minute. But he seems calmer at dinner, and even Prem sat quietly with him last Sunday.

qa.q: What did Sunaina once hear Manoj whisper?
qa.a: She heard him whisper, "Thank you for the rain and for Amma's dal."

qa.q: What might Manoj be feeling during his quiet minute?
qa.a: He may feel grateful and peaceful, thankful for simple things like the rain and his mother's dal.

qa.q: How could the family support Manoj's new habit?
qa.a: They could give him that quiet minute without teasing, and maybe share one thing they are grateful for at dinner.

qa.q: How does Prem's reaction change over time?
qa.a: Prem first teases Manoj about being a monk but later sits quietly with him, as if he has started to respect or enjoy it.

grounding: Shows a child taking up a short silent gratitude practice at the family table.
